articles.title: India sitting on 'economic disaster': Rahul Gandhi at Columbia University
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Current Affairs: Bilateral Agreements, Foreign Visits & UN/G20/BRICS
fullParagraphs: Leader of the Opposition in the Lok Sabha Rahul Gandhi said the country’s economic model ceased to deliver results nearly a decade ago, leaving it with a deepening employment crisis and a weakened manufacturing base.

Speaking at a fireside chat at Columbia University on Tuesday (November 17, 2026), moderated by New York Times journalist Lydia Polgreen, Mr. Gandhi said India is sitting on an “economic disaster” that could become far more serious if the country continued on its present course.
“The blunt thing is that India is sitting on an economic disaster. That’s the reality of it,” he said.

“One can brush it aside, the media can brush it aside. But India has got a massive unemployment problem. India’s got a massive problem with its education system. And these are things you cannot get away from,” he added.

Mr. Gandhi identified small and medium businesses, agriculture and manufacturing as the backbone and principal engines of job creation, arguing that the services sector could not absorb India’s expanding workforce.

“The spine of the economy is small and medium business, which is the job creation engine, and agriculture. That is fundamental in India and required. The spine of the economy has been broken,” he said.

The Opposition leader said India could not achieve sustainable economic development without rebuilding its manufacturing capabilities. “We cannot survive successfully without manufacturing, it just cannot be done,” he said.
Mr. Gandhi alleged that economic growth was concentrated in a few large business groups while smaller enterprises were struggling.

“Why is there no private investment in India? Why are the only people who are growing in India, businesses that are growing in India called Adani and Ambani? Why is Tata literally being taken over by Mr. [Gautam] Adani?” he asked.

Mr. Gandhi placed the recent student-led Gen Z protests alongside resistance movements by Adivasis, Dalits and farmers against what he called the growing concentration of political and economic power in the last decade. He said the student-led protests showed that fear of “coercive power of the State” didn’t work.

“There’s a massive concentration of wealth taking place in India, and huge disenfranchisement of people. Vote is just one element of it,” he said, alleging that tribal land was being taken without consultation and that minorities, Dalits and farmers were facing growing marginalisation.

Referring to youth unemployment and economic difficulties in the U.S. and European countries, including Germany and Britain, Mr. Gandhi argued their economic challenges are serious and India’s relatively lower costs offer resilience, he said.

articles.title: Scientists warn of growing health threats of chemicals found everywhere
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Prelims: ISRO/NASA Missions, Defense Updates, Tech & Climate Reports
fullParagraphs: Chemicals found almost everywhere in modern life pose a "global and growing threat" to human health and the environment, a landmark report based on over a decade of research has warned.

The report on "endocrine-disrupting chemicals" (EDCs) released by the United Nations Environment Programme and World Health Organization "conservatively" estimates the health and environmental costs of EDC exposure at over $1 trillion annually.

"The scientific evidence is clear: EDCs are a global and growing threat to human and environmental health," warns the report written by international scientists, calling current regulations "uneven and insufficient."
EDCs are chemicals that interfere with, mimic, or block the hormones that regulate the development and behaviour of our organs.
They are in everything from toys and makeup, to building materials and clothing.
The report released late Tuesday is the first such comprehensive look at EDC impacts in 14 years, and finds increasingly clear links between them and a range of diseases.
"The evidence is so strong that it's irrefutable at this point," said Laura Vandenberg, report co-author and professor of environmental health sciences at the University of Massachusetts Amherst.
The report examined thousands of studies on chemicals like bisphenols, phthalates and parabens.
Evidence of links between these chemicals and disease is strongest for certain neurological conditions and reproductive problems including sperm decline.
But there is also growing confidence that EDCs are linked to diseases like type 2 diabetes and asthma that have spiked globally.
"Because these changes are occurring rapidly, they are unlikely to be explained primarily by genetic change," the report says.
Scientists looked at associations between EDC exposure and health conditions, as well as the mechanisms by which exposure could cause harm.

articles.title: Researchers boost gut microbial activity linked to longevity in aged mice, find improved metabolism
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Prelims: ISRO/NASA Missions, Defense Updates, Tech & Climate Reports
fullParagraphs: Researchers have identified changes in the metabolic activity of the gut microbiome associated with exceptional longevity in humans, and found that amplifying the same activity in aged mice using engineered bacteria improved metabolic health.

Published in the journal Cell Metabolism , the team's study suggests that specific age-related changes in the gut microbiome may be protective adaptations rather than signs of decline, and could potentially be harnessed to support healthier aging.

Senior author Amir Zarrinpar, chair in circadian biology and medicine, and professor of medicine at the University of California San Diego, said while many studies on aging focus on what goes wrong as one grows old, the findings suggest "some changes in the gut microbiome may actually represent the body's attempt to preserve metabolic health".
"If we can identify those beneficial functions and safely strengthen them, we may eventually be able to develop new ways to promote healthier aging," Zarrinpar said.

The gut microbiome, the community of bacteria and other microbes living in the digestive tract, is known to change throughout life and plays an important role in metabolism and inflammation, among other aspects of health.
Studies have also found distinctive microbiome features among people who age exceptionally well.
The researchers focused on how gut microbes modify bile acids, substances produced by the liver that help digest fats but also act as signalling molecules in the body.

Studying young and aged mice, they found that aging was associated with an increased microbial activity linked to enzymes called bile salt hydrolases. These enzymes chemically modify bile acids, allowing them to influence pathways involved in metabolism, inflammation and the body's internal clock.
The team also found greater bile acid modification in the mice.
To determine patterns in humans, they reanalysed publicly available data from a human ageing cohort, analysing bile acid measurements from 48 young adults, 107 older adults and 125 centenarians.

The centenarian group showed higher ratios of modified bile acids than both younger groups. An analysis of microbiome data also revealed a greater abundance of a gene associated with bile salt hydrolase activity among centenarians compared with the older adult group.
Further, aged mice -- 82-week-old mice -- were introduced with a strain of bacteria native to the gut engineered to continuously produce bile salt hydrolases.

articles.title: Does India need to financially aid families’ decisions to have a child through fertility treatment?
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Prelims: ISRO/NASA Missions, Defense Updates, Tech & Climate Reports
fullParagraphs: The reproductive-autonomy jurisprudence as evolved by the Supreme Court under Article 21 of the Constitution is rich yet narrow, focusing primarily on one side of the problem. In Suchita Srivastava v. Chandigarh Administration (2009), the Court held that reproductive choices may be exercised to procreate as well as to abstain from procreating. In X v. Principal Secretary, Health and Family Welfare Department (2022), the Supreme Court extended the right to abortion to unmarried women as an exercise of ‘decisional autonomy’.

These, and nearly all other landmark cases are concerned only with an existing pregnancy. The freedom to pursue parenthood through medical treatment, however, has surfaced only at the margins. The Delhi High Court, in 2023, allowed parole of a life convict to attempt IVF, by recognising a “right to parenthood,” but only as a claim against a barrier the State itself had erected. No court has yet asked whether the State may leave a citizen’s access to infertility care entirely to their own purse. Can a right available to the fertile but structurally withheld from the infertile be called a universal right?

articles.title: Cyclone Akvan: why is Andhra Pradesh facing a third cyclone in a month?
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Prelims: ISRO/NASA Missions, Defense Updates, Tech & Climate Reports
fullParagraphs: Andhra Pradesh is currently facing a rare weather phenomenon. Since October 28, the State has already been hit by two back-to-back cyclonic storms, and there is an imminent threat of another one battering the coastal districts in the next two days.

On October 28, the State was battered by very severe cyclonic storm Arnab , which made landfall near Narsapur in West Godavari district. On November 3, it was hit again by severe cyclonic storm Murasu , which made landfall close to Ongole in Prakasam district. Now, cyclonic storm Akvan is likely to intensify into a very severe cyclonic storm and make landfall on November 20 between Narsapur and Puri.

Three tropical storms battering the coast within less than a month during the post-monsoon season is a rare scenario. The last times such a thing happened were in 1976, 1987 and 2013. Both 1976 and 1987 were El Niño years, and this year is also categorised as a super El Niño year .

When it comes to tropical cyclones over the Bay of Bengal, there are a number of driving factors, and El Niño is just one of them. Mostly, the formation of storms over the Bay, especially their frequency and intensity, differs slightly from the rest of the world, because the Bay of Bengal is almost a land-locked sea, said S.S.V.S. Ramakrishna, former head of the Department of Oceanography and Meteorology, Andhra University, who has spent over four decades researching the pattern of cyclones over the Bay.
“El Niño typically suppresses the southwest summer monsoon over India, but it has the opposite effect on the Northeast (winter) Monsoon and post-monsoon cyclogenesis in the Bay of Bengal,” he said.

During El Niño years, the northeast monsoon tends to be significantly more active over southern peninsular India. This creates continuous moisture convergence and frequent convective disturbances over the southern Bay, providing a steady assembly line of low-pressure areas.

And sometimes, in rare occurrences, remnants of a Pacific Ocean cyclone cross the Strait of Malacca, re-enter the Bay of Bengal, and intensify into a cyclone. “We had seen this phenomenon during the Odisha Super Cyclone in 1999,” he said.

Mr. Ramakrishna also pointed out that in October and November, the Bay of Bengal consistently retained high sea surface temperatures—over 26.5 degrees Celsius—and anything above 26 is conducive to developing a cyclonic system. This has been aided by the El Niño-modified upper-level wind patterns over the southern Bay of Bengal, which reduce vertical wind shear.

Another key factor that acted as a catalyst is the massive freshwater discharge from rivers like the Ganga, Brahmaputra and Godavari into the Bay of Bengal, which resulted in creating a low-salinity surface layer. This acts as a “barrier layer” that prevents cooler, deeper ocean water from mixing upward, so a passing cyclone (like Arnab or Murasu) does not cool the sea surface enough to stop the next storm from forming days later.

Persistent upper-tropospheric ridges (anticyclonic circulations) over the China–Myanmar region and central India have acted as steering barriers, blocking storms from recurving northeast and forcing them northwestward into the Andhra coast, he said.

articles.title: Air purifier sales surge as demand, smart features drive market growth
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Prelims: ISRO/NASA Missions, Defense Updates, Tech & Climate Reports
fullParagraphs: Demand for air purifiers in India has witnessed explosive growth in 2026, with major brands and retail platforms reporting sales doubling or tripling year-on-year. Driven by an early surge ahead of the traditional winter pollution season , consumer behaviour is shifting toward viewing indoor air quality as a year-round health priority rather than an emergency seasonal purchase.
According to industry leaders, adoption is gaining momentum well before peak pollution months.

Smart tech brand Qubo recorded a 150 percent growth over the previous year, while Xiaomi registered approximately 3X year-on-year sales growth during the festive period. Industry executives note that growing awareness surrounding indoor pollutants, ranging from dust and pet dander to everyday cooking and cleaning emissions, is encouraging households to take a proactive approach to home wellness throughout the year.

Retail footprint and online traffic reflect this expanding market footprint across the country. Electronics retailer Croma reported that air purifier sales volumes have more than doubled in 2026. While Delhi-NCR remains the dominant market, cities like Mumbai and regions beyond traditional high-pollution belts are showing sustained upticks.
Premium tech maker Dyson also reported that visits to its air purifier pages grew by over 100 percent in October compared to the same period last year.

Modern buyers are increasingly seeking advanced functionality and intelligent filtration tech. Croma highlighted strong consumer interest in models featuring real-time AQI displays, app controls, and multi-functional units combining purification with humidification or heating.

On e-commerce platforms, Amazon India reported that sales doubled over the past week. Shoppers are actively leveraging Rufus, Amazon’s personalised AI shopping assistant, to filter models by room size, filter type, and live sensor capabilities, prompting the e-retailer to expand selection on Amazon Now for immediate delivery.

“We have observed a notable increase in consumer demand for air purifiers on Flipkart, reflected in higher search activity, product discovery and purchases. Northern India continues to account for a significant share of demand for the category. We also witnessed a rise in purchases during the early hours following Diwali, coinciding with heightened concerns around deteriorating air quality and the steps households are taking to manage their indoor environments,” said Flipkart.

articles.title: NASA Voyager 1 probe believed to have reached ‘light-day’ milestone
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Prelims: ISRO/NASA Missions, Defense Updates, Tech & Climate Reports
fullParagraphs: NASA’s Voyager 1 probe is believed to have now ​hit a distance milestone accomplished by no other spacecraft from Earth, based ⁠on advance computations by the U.S. space agency, as the probe ventures through the near-emptiness of interstellar space.

The robotic probe, launched in 1977, was calculated by NASA to have reached a light-day from Earth, ‌the distance that light travels in 24 hours — about 16 billion miles (26 billion km) — on Wednesday (November 18, 2026) at 5:16 a.m. ET (1016 GMT).
Infographic | Voyager I — A five-decade journey to get one light-day away

Officials at NASA’s Jet Propulsion ‌Laboratory in California will have to wait about a day to get a ‌signal ⁠from the probe, confirming it has reached this distance. They have scheduled an event ⁠for Thursday (November 19) to discuss the milestone.
“Reaching one light-day is an astounding feat, one that I never expected to see,” Voyager project manager Suzanne Dodd said.

Voyager 1, the most distant human-made object, is flying at almost 38,000 ​miles per hour (61,000 kph). It crossed ‌the outer edge of the heliosphere, a protective bubble of particles and magnetic fields produced by the sun, to enter interstellar space in 2012. Its twin, Voyager 2, was also launched in 1977 and entered interstellar space in 2018.
A Jet Propulsion Laboratory representative ‌said recent power-saving measures could give the two Voyager spacecraft enough power to stay in ​communication with Earth for three to four more years.

“But the goal of the mission is to do science, and there is enough power to ⁠keep the current suite of instruments going through the 50th launch anniversary next year. Beyond that is hard to predict, and of course these are nearly 50-year-old spacecraft, and there are ‌always things the team cannot anticipate that might happen,” the JPL representative said.

Voyager 1 journeyed past Jupiter and Saturn, the solar system’s two largest planets, earlier in its mission. It continues to gather scientific data. For instance, its instruments have detected the faint monotonous hum caused by the constant vibrations of the small amounts of gas present in interstellar space.

“Voyager is sending back continuous measurements of magnetic fields, cosmic rays and of plasma waves that we ‌receive on Earth whenever the Deep Space Network points its antenna at Voyager,” Mr. Dodd said.
The Deep Space Network ​is NASA’s international array of giant radio antennas supporting interplanetary spacecraft missions.

“After the heliopause crossing, the magnetic field direction did not rotate into the interstellar direction ⁠as expected, but has maintained the direction it had when both Voyagers crossed the heliopause, a direction ⁠governed by our sun. We are watching to see when that rotation might occur,” Mr. Dodd said.

articles.title: Elusive peace: On Kashmir terror attack
articles.examRelevance: UPSC & State PSC Mains / Essay: Deep Analytical Core Summary & Vocabulary
fullParagraphs: Three months of lull established by security forces in Jammu and Kashmir was rattled by the back-to-back incidents of violence in the past six days. On November 11, a terror attack on a checkpoint manned by the personnel of the Central Reserve Police Force (CRPF) in Kulgam left three jawans injured. On November 16, a local, whom the police suspected of having joined the terror ranks a few days ago, was killed after six days of a siege-like anti-terror operation in residential areas of Kulgam. In Jammu’s Kishtwar, two Special Police Officers (SPOs) of the J&K Police were found dead with bullet wounds, a day after they were reported missing in a forest range on November 11. The police and the Army, however, remain tight-lipped about the circumstances around the killing of these SPOs, and there are conflicting reports on the circumstances that led to their deaths. The anti-terror operation in civilian areas of Kulgam has raised concerns. Former J&K Chief Minister and PDP president Mehbooba Mufti described the operation, spread over six days, as “collective punishment that only breeds alienation and resentment,” while NC spokesman Imran Nabi Dar suggested that entire villages were put under prolonged restrictions for days. The Omar Abdullah government , because of limited powers and no jurisdiction over the police in J&K, a Union Territory since 2019, finds itself hamstrung. The iron hand policy to stamp out terrorism and separatism has been effective from a strictly security perspective — terror attacks as well as local recruitments into terror ranks have declined. According to the police, local recruits have come down to single digit or fewer than 10 in Kashmir.

That said, the decline in terrorist incidents and the silence of the streets should not be mistaken for peace. The current situation demands a political reach-out by the Centre to all the stakeholders of J&K. It has to begin with the much-promised restoration of Statehood , which will give the voters a sense that their mass participation in the 2024 Assembly elections allowed their elected leaders to hold institutions accountable, and they were able to work freely to protect the interests of the region. Though the security agencies need to be focused on Pakistan-backed terrorism, it should not come at the cost of re-inflicting psychological scars within Kashmir, which could turn into a powder keg if left unattended. Healing through both political and security processes has to be complementary rather than conflicting. Allowing the political class of J&K to establish its writ and providing room to security agencies to combat challenges are not contradictory.

articles.title: All-too fallible: On India’s vote against moratorium on death penalty
articles.examRelevance: UPSC & State PSC Mains / Essay: Deep Analytical Core Summary & Vocabulary
fullParagraphs: India’s vote against a proposed global moratorium on the death penalty at the UN is consistent with its position at the forum; it has defended its retention of the penalty as a sovereign decision backed by judicial safeguards, including the “rarest of rare” condition and sessions courts’ sentences requiring a High Court’s confirmation. At the same time, the Supreme Court has increasingly restricted capital punishment and research has failed to find evidence of additional deterrence over life imprisonment . India’s distinction between judicial executions and extrajudicial killings is legally valid but its further claim that due process protects people facing execution is less so. While India last executed convicts in 2020, for the Delhi gang-rape and murder, Parliament expanded the number of capital offences under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita — a form of penal populism that projects the political attractiveness of the state’s response to public outrage, especially in cases of sexual violence, without addressing the poor policing and low conviction rates that actually undermine deterrence . The country had 574 people on death row on December 31, 2025, the highest since 2016, thanks to trial court rulings, challenging claims about judicial safeguards in practice. The report of the 2015 Law Commission headed by Justice A.P. Shah said the death penalty “fails to achieve any constitutionally valid penological goals” and recommended abolishing it for all crimes except terrorism and waging war.

Only a small group of countries worldwide are executing more people. In India, per Project 39A, the Supreme Court released 38 persons from death row in 2016-2025 after they had spent eight years there on average. Some have endured more than two decades. The punishment requires a measure of infallibility that the criminal justice system cannot supply. The safeguards neither deter convictions in cases with flawed evidence, false testimony, and so on nor remedy unequal access to competent legal representation among those facing the penalty. India should formally suspend executions and commission a review of penalty statutes and the treatment of prisoners on death row. Second, it should spare offences that do not involve intentional killing from the penalty. Research suggests meting out excessively harsh punishments for non-fatal crimes could incentivise offenders to escalate their violence, including to kill potential witnesses. The greater goal should be to abolish the practice in law while improving investigative and prosecutorial practices and access to legal aid.

articles.title: Outlook outage: On Microsoft and dangers of centralising digital systems
articles.examRelevance: UPSC & State PSC Mains / Essay: Deep Analytical Core Summary & Vocabulary
fullParagraphs: Last week, Microsoft’s suite of productivity and email software, which businesses, governments, hospitals and a host of other organisations rely upon round-the-clock, abruptly stopped working globally , affecting tens of millions of people around the world. The company has cited a network upgrade gone awry as the root cause of the incident. Incidents such as the Microsoft 365 outage are a natural consequence of businesses and governments allowing key digital systems to become centralised all over the world. The internet remains, and was pioneered as, a network of networks. If one business’s networks went down, the reasoning went, others would not fall like dominos: everyone was, after all, connected to everyone else. But the economics have long been prohibitive, with dedicated servers and web-connected infrastructure infeasible for all but the largest businesses, with even those firms seeking the enticing cost savings from socialised infrastructure. That made sense: the internet made shared infrastructure more economical, allowing hardware and maintenance costs to be spread so far and wide that at a per-user level prices have been negligible. Competition among major cloud providers, the few that remain at Microsoft’s scale, have kept prices affordable for enterprise software for all shades of organisations.

Digital services have grown more sophisticated, and more deeply integrated into the economy as this centralisation unfolded. But the downside is that, regardless of the sophistication and professionalism of any company, mistakes happen, and the scale of these mistakes can quickly cascade over to the entire economy. There are societal and organisational lessons to be gleaned from these episodes. There is no such thing as a reliable vendor. Governments must also draw a cyber sovereignty lesson here that does not simply entail swapping a global vendor for a domestic one. It is the subversion of the internet’s architecture that is at the root of these incidents. Investing in resilience — and shielding critical operations from destabilising disruptions, no matter how improbable — should inform attitudes to digital systems. As a new generation of AI data centres is poised to supercharge the centralised systems of yesteryear, it is all the more imperative to mitigate even occasional vagaries of large systems.

articles.title: Clear the path: On SCO Civilisational Dialogue Forum in New Delhi
articles.examRelevance: UPSC & State PSC Mains / Essay: Deep Analytical Core Summary & Vocabulary
fullParagraphs: While maintaining its hard stance on cross-border terrorism, India has an opportunity to recognise that many of its other interests still merit sustained cooperation with Pakistan as the latter’s climate minister Musadik Masood Malik prepares to attend the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) Civilisational Dialogue Forum in New Delhi. India’s official position since the Pahalgam attack and the ensuing confrontations along the border is that terrorism and bilateral talks cannot coexist. A month later, Prime Minister Narendra Modi signalled that India’s relations with Pakistan would remain subordinate to its demands on cross-border terrorism by extending the condition to trade and water. South Asia is already one of the least economically integrated regions worldwide, with intra-regional trade at around 5%, and, as Chatham House has inferred, strained ties between India and its neighbours have created diplomatic vacuums that Beijing has taken advantage of through trilateral and regional groupings. Now, by inviting all SCO members to the national capital and participating in meetings ahead of the August 2027 Islamabad Summit, New Delhi has shown some maturity as a convening power. Islamabad is also being pragmatic in keeping channels open during its SCO chairmanship by participating in an initiative championed by Mr. Modi.

The pursuit of regionwide water security remains particularly fluid, with India seemingly overlooking the fact that it is upstream of Pakistan and Bangladesh and downstream of China. After India stopped sharing routine hydrological data of the Indus river and approved the Chenab-Beas link tunnel project, Mr. Malik fanned the flames saying Pakistan would “cut off those hands” seeking to restrict its share of the water. Yet China has now restricted the same data vis-à-vis the Brahmaputra while it builds the Medog mega-dam in Tibet. India has also protested the proposed Padma Barrage in Bangladesh, which has been increasing its alignment with China, echoing India building the Farakka Barrage over East Pakistan’s objections in 1961. Climate change is rendering cooperation more essential to manage the integrity of contested geographies, the willingness of border populations to engage, and the potential to generate hydroelectric power. New Delhi should retreat from the notion that working together on the Indus will be a concession to Islamabad and see in the Dialogue an opportunity to restore the necessary channels. Suspending ties may communicate political resolve but will not diminish terrorists’ capabilities in the region or improve India’s security. It has already compromised India’s ambitions to regional leadership, which require the ability to keep engaging even with difficult neighbours. India should go beyond using multilateral fora to assert its national position and start identifying areas where bilateral cooperation serves its interests, including with Pakistan.

articles.title: A step back: On Trump’s no-war, no-deal approach against Iran
articles.examRelevance: UPSC & State PSC Mains / Essay: Deep Analytical Core Summary & Vocabulary
fullParagraphs: Before the November 3 midterm elections, U.S. President Donald Trump had repeatedly threatened to “destroy” Iran unless it entered into a deal with the U.S. to end the war. Since the elections, in which Mr. Trump’s Republican Party suffered a massive defeat , the U.S. President appears to have toned down his rhetoric. Last week, he said he had decided against escalating the military conflict with Iran following requests from America’s Gulf allies. But the U.S. would maintain the naval blockade of the Islamic Republic. Mr. Trump also pulled Vice President J.D. Vance off negotiations with Iran, as the Qatar-mediated talks made no real progress. Iran wants the U.S. to lift the blockade, unfreeze its frozen assets, issue sanctions relief and pull back from the Persian Gulf for direct negotiations on the nuclear programme to restart. The U.S., which calls Iran’s demands “outrageous”, has now adopted a no-war, no-deal approach , hoping that the economic blockade would force Tehran to offer concessions in the near future. Mr. Trump’s retreat from the threats reflects the realities on the ground. Before the U.S. and Israel launched this war by assassinating Iran’s Supreme Leader on February 28, Tehran was ready to make concessions. The U.S. and Israel carried out heavy bombing for 40 days but achieved none of their declared objectives. There is no guarantee that another round of strikes would force Iran to change its position. And the war, as the midterm results show, remains very unpopular in America.

Mr. Trump has only himself, and Benjamin Netanyahu, to blame for the predicament he is in. He is the one who sabotaged a functioning Obama-era nuclear deal in 2018 that had denied Iran a path towards the nuclear bomb. Mr. Trump joined Israel’s unprovoked war on Iran in June 2025 and declared that he had “obliterated” Iran’s nuclear programme. And the same Mr. Trump started the current war, just eight months later, over the same nuclear programme. The Iranian state has survived, though Iranians are facing enormous economic woes. Tehran shut the Strait of Hormuz, pumping up global energy prices. Iran’s counterattacks have either destroyed or damaged America’s bases in the Persian Gulf. High oil prices and inflation turned the American electorate against the Republican party, while in Israel, Mr. Netanyahu, despite war rhetoric and racist attacks on the country’s Arab minorities, lost the governing majority. The setbacks are there for anyone to see. Yet, Mr. Trump does not seem to have grasped the seriousness of the situation. His no-war, no-deal approach r isks a resumption of hostilities as Iran has pledged to break the siege. The U.S. has few clear military options unless it is prepared to launch a ground invasion, which would be disastrous. A more rational way forward is to end the war through diplomacy. But for that, Mr. Trump must first accept the strategic reality that he has lost the war.

articles.title: Stoop to conquer: On the Opposition’s seat-sharing ahead of U.P. polls

fullParagraphs: As Uttar Pradesh heads to the polls in early 2027, a familiar seat-sharing tussle has emerged within the Opposition. The Samajwadi Party and the Congress share an understanding forged during the Lok Sabha elections that earned them a good share of the State’s seats, but the Congress is now reportedly seeking 181 seats , nearly 45% of the 403 Assembly constituencies. It is the latest instance of the dilemma facing the Congress as it seeks revival in States where it has become a marginal force: how to strike a favourable bargain with stronger partners without weakening the coalition against the Bharatiya Janata Party. With discontent rising against the BJP, which still occupies a hegemonic position in the party system , the Opposition feels a wind behind its sails, and its major parties agree that the only way to take on the BJP is a formidable coalition with a compelling, unified message. But the Congress’s attempt to rebuild itself in the Hindi heartland and in States where it once held sway has strained that unity. In Bihar, the Mahagathbandhan failed to reap the benefits of anti-incumbency against the Janata Dal (United)-BJP alliance, partly because it could not tap the full support of the social forces behind the Rashtriya Janata Dal and the Congress, and partly because the Congress took too long to settle seat-sharing for the campaigns to gel. In Tamil Nadu, the Congress held out for more seats from the Dravida Munnetra Kazhagam and delayed the alliance, while infighting produced a lacklustre campaign that left it with the lowest vote share, in the seats it contested, among the alliance partners.

Uttar Pradesh need not go the same way. The demand for 181 seats is overly ambitious for a party that managed a mere 2.33% of the votes in the 399 seats it contested in 2022, when the SP won 111 of the 347 seats it contested with a 32% vote share. The Congress has a point that the variables have changed since. In 2024, the SP and the Congress together won 43 of U.P.‘s 80 Lok Sabha seats with a 43.2% vote share, just short of the BJP-led alliance’s 43.7%. The Congress won only six of the 17 seats it contested, but its vote share in those six, 44.2%, was marginally ahead of the SP’s 43.4%. The party could also argue that its national campaigns on youth concerns and the state of India’s electoral democracy give it the heft to seek more. But its lack of an efficient State-wide organisation suggests that 181 is too high. The SP remains the strongest Opposition party , having assiduously built a new social coalition of backward classes, Dalits and minorities to take on the majoritarian BJP through local mobilisations. The 2024 arrangement, in which the Congress contested a fifth of the seats, is a more reasonable guide. A well-targeted 100 or so seats would make for a more coherent campaign and a better showing alongside the SP.

articles.title: A period of good governance, says CM; a betrayal of people says Pinarayi
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II: Polity, Governance, Supreme Court Judgements, Bills & Govt Schemes
fullParagraphs: Keralam Chief Minister V. D. Satheesan and the Leader of the Opposition Pinarayi Vijayan have expressed divergent views on six months of Congress-led United Democratic Front (UDF) government.

Mr. Satheesan sought to paint a rosy picture of good governance, development, welfare, and fulfilled promises. He has claimed a 28 per cent increase in tax revenue. The UDF has also rolled out politically popular goodies, including free travel for women on State transport buses, priority ration cards for financially hard-pressed families, a senior citizens welfare programme and a hike in the honorarium of scheme workers, pre-primary teachers and child carers in anganwadis.

He has also claimed that the government was focused on laying the groundwork for a “New Age Keralam”. The government also touted its legislative successes in passing laws to improve the ease of doing business, slash red tape, and provide investors with a transparent, single-window clearance mechanism.

Mr. Satheesan also dwelt at length on his flagship programme, Mission Samudra, a ₹400 crore maritime development initiative. He has sought to cast the commencement of Export-Import (EXIM) operations from the Vizhinjam International Sea Port as his government’s signature achievement.

Mr. Satheesan also promised citizens two international sea ports, 18 mini airports, aviation-linked industries, and more tech parks to transform Keralam into an economic powerhouse. He promised lakhs of new jobs for Keralam’s educated youth by 2031.
Mr Satheesan also projected Operation Toofan, the law enforcement anti-drug enforcement drive, as an administrative achievement.
In stark contrast, Mr. Vijayan was scathingly critical of the UDF government, calling Mr. Satheesan’s six months of governance a betrayal of the people.

Mr. Vijayan said Mr. Satheesan had “put up Keralam for sale”, opening the door to corruption, including hasty agreements with private entities to purchase electricity at exaggerated rates, citing a “non-existent” power scarcity and dishonestly raising the spectre of economically crippling power cuts.

He accused the UDF of sacrificing the welfare of the coastal community at the altar of mercantilism. He said the UDF had opened the floodgates of environmental exploitation by allowing corporate players to exploit Keralam’s rare earths, including mineral-rich beaches, the fragile marine ecosystem, and green-flagged deep-sea mining.

articles.title: Cyclone Akvan moves slowly, likely to intensify further by November 18 morning
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II: Polity, Governance, Supreme Court Judgements, Bills & Govt Schemes
fullParagraphs: Cyclonic storm Akvan (meaning ‘demon’ in Persian) over the central parts of the south and west-central Bay of Bengal may intensify into a severe cyclonic storm by Wednesday morning.

Initially, the India Meteorological Department (IMD) forecast that the weather system would strengthen into a severe cyclonic storm by Tuesday evening, but the system had either remained stationary or moved slowly.

At 5.30 p.m., the weather system was centred around 590 km east of Chennai in Tamil Nadu, 630 km northeast of Trincomalee in Sri Lanka, 650 km southeast of Machilipatnam and 650 km south-southeast of Visakhapatnam in Andhra Pradesh and 780 km south of Gopalpur in Odisha.

It may continue to move slowly north-northwestwards and intensify into a severe cyclonic storm over west-central Bay of Bengal on Wednesday morning, and further into a very severe cyclonic storm by Thursday morning.

The system has changed its track slightly, and the probable landfall points may remain between Visakhapatnam and Nellore. Isolated heavy rainfall is likely in the northern districts of Visakhapatnam, Alluri Sitharama Raju, Parvathipuram Manyam, Srikakulam, Vizianagaram, and strong winds with speeds of 100 kmph to 110 kmph are likely along the coastal belt from Wednesday evening.

Andhra Pradesh is experiencing a very rare event, since it is not often that a State sees three tropical cyclones crossing its coast within a month, said IMD Director General of Meteorology Mrutyunjay Mohapatra.

Speaking to The Hindu over the phone, he said it is normal for the Bay of Bengal to see three or four tropical cyclones in a year. “What is not normal is that all of them are crossing the coast near Andhra Pradesh.”

A similar event last happened in 1987. And, the reason for this can be attributed to El Nino, he said. “Both 1987 and 2026 have strong similarities. 1987 was a strong El Nino year, with drought conditions. And 2026 is one too,” he said.
Mr. Mohapatra explained that El Nino influences the formation of cyclones in such a way that more of these develop over the southern latitude, which may move towards A.P.
Handling a disaster of this kind has become challenging for the State.

Andhra Pradesh State Disaster Management Authority (APSDMA) Managing Director and Real Time Governance Society (RTGS) CEO Prakhar Jain called the situation unprecedented. “It is challenging for the government to deal with a third cyclone, Akvan, while still dealing with the aftermath of Arnab and Murasu. A lot of restoration work is underway, and another cyclone at this time adds to the challenges,” Mr. Jain said.
The water retention capacity of soil may also be compromised due to extremely heavy rainfall triggered by the previous two cyclones.

articles.title: World needs peace, stability, predictability: Modi in Manila
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II: Polity, Governance, Supreme Court Judgements, Bills & Govt Schemes
fullParagraphs: Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Tuesday (November 17, 2026) called for “peace, stability, and predictability” in the world as he attended the ASEAN-India Summit, the East Asia Summit, and the Quad Leaders’ Summit in Manila, Philippines. He made a number of proposals aimed at maritime security, protecting critical minerals supply chains, and enhancing trade.

The Quad Summit, which was being held for the first time in a non-member country, was hosted by U.S. President Donald Trump and was also attended by Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese and Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi, apart from Mr. Modi. The leaders issued a joint statement opposing economic and maritime “coercion” in the Indo-Pacific, and Mr. Modi announced that India would host the first Quad Business Forum in Mumbai in 2027.

The three back-to-back events had started with Mr. Modi’s meeting with the leaders of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) for the ASEAN-India Summit, where the Prime Minister said the world now needed peace, stability, and predictability more than ever.

“Together, India and ASEAN represent nearly one-fourth of the world’s population. That is why it is essential to ensure that our future is shaped not by competition, but by cooperation,” Mr. Modi told the leaders of Brunei, Cambodia, Indonesia, Laos, Malaysia, the Philippines, Singapore, Thailand, Timor-Leste, and Vietnam. Myanmar’s military junta leader, President Min Aung Laing, was not invited, and the country was represented by an official.
At the event, he also promised that India would give e-visas free of charge to ASEAN tourists.

Prime Minister Narendra Modi, Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr., and ASEAN leaders pose for an official family photo at the 23rd India-ASEAN Summit, in Manila on Tuesday. Photo: Narendra Modi Photo Gallery/ANI Photo

Following this, Mr. Modi took part in the East Asia Summit, which was attended by the leaders of India, China, Russia, the U.S., Japan, South Korea, and the ASEAN countries. At this summit, he proposed a seafarers’ safety initiative. He said that “whether it is the conflict in Ukraine or West Asia, India will continue to support every effort towards peace”.

The East Asia Summit members also issued a joint declaration on tackling cyber-crime, given the number of online fraud cases originating from Southeast Asian countries. India will host a summit on the issue at the National Forensic Sciences University in Gandhinagar and an East Asia Summit University Heads Conclave at Nalanda.

In this image received on Nov. 17, 2026, Prime Minister Narendra Modi poses for a group photograph with Philippines' President Ferdinand Marcos Jr., and other world leaders, during 21st East Asia Summit, part of the 49th ASEAN Summit, in Manila, Philippines. Photo: PMO via PTI Photo
The ASEAN engagements were important as Mr. Modi had skipped the summits in Malaysia last year.

Shortly before he left Manila, the Prime Minister met the leaders of the U.S., Australia, and Japan for the Quad Summit, which was last held in 2024. This was the first time that all the Quad leaders have met since the U.S.-Israel attacks on Iran and the blockade in the Strait of Hormuz began more than nine months ago — in a war where at least 23 Indians, mainly seafarers, have been killed.

From left, Japan's Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi, Prime Minister Narendra Modi, President Donald Trump and Australia's Prime Minister Anthony Albanese prepare fro a group photo during the meeting of the leaders of the Quad in Manila, Philippines, on November 17, 2026. | Photo Credit: AP

articles.title: Allahabad High Court grants interim bail to Azam Khan, terms arrest by ED as ‘motivated and mala fide’
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II: Polity, Governance, Supreme Court Judgements, Bills & Govt Schemes
fullParagraphs: The Allahabad High Court on Tuesday (November 17, 2026) granted interim bail to former Uttar Pradesh Minister and Samajwadi Party (SP) leader Mohammad Azam Khan, observing that the arrest of Mr. Khan by the Enforcement Directorate (ED) was “motivated and mala fide ”.

A Division Bench of Justices Rajiv Gupta and Devendra Singh directed Mr. Khan’s release, noting that the Central agency had prima facie failed to follow the mandatory procedure while arresting him in a money laundering case.

“....the petitioner was taken into custody in the instant case moments after he was physically released from the jail in another case (PAN Card Case) after furnishing bail bonds and sureties on 31.2.2026 at 7:10 p.m. at the jail gate itself, which clearly underlines the motivated and malafide nature of the present proceedings,” the High Court said.
The relief will remain in force until the next hearing, scheduled for December 10, 2026.

It further noted that the ED had apparently not provided Mr. Khan with written grounds of arrest before producing him before the court for remand. Also, the arrest memo and the reasons for his arrest did not appear to have been properly communicated to him.

Mr. Khan was arrested on October 31, 2026, shortly after he was released from Rampur District Jail in another case involving allegations related to dual PAN cards. He had secured bail in that case from the Allahabad High Court on October 29, and was physically released after furnishing bail bonds and sureties on October 31. However, the ED arrested him again at the gate of the jail at around 7.10 p.m.

Challenging his arrest, Mr. Khan argued that the ED had violated his fundamental rights under Article 22(1) of the Constitution and Section 19 of the Prevention of Money Laundering Act (PMLA), which lay down safeguards that must be followed during an arrest.

His counsel, senior advocate Kapil Sibal, told the court that the written grounds of arrest were neither handed over to Mr. Khan at the time of arrest nor provided before he was produced for remand the following day. The ED had claimed that its officers tried to hand over the documents but Khan refused to accept them.

The court further observed that although the ED claimed to have videographed the arrest, it had not produced any video or photograph showing its officers offering the documents to Mr. Khan, and him refusing to accept them. The court also noted that the ED had not mentioned the alleged videography in its remand application.
The ED’s explanation required further examination and directed both sides to exchange affidavits before the next hearing, the court said.

The ED’s money-laundering investigation centres on alleged financial irregularities and illegal occupation of farmers’ agricultural land linked to the Rampur-based Mohammad Ali Jauhar University. The agency has alleged that funds and materials allocated for public projects were diverted to the university, government works were carried out on its private campus, and donations to the Mohammad Ali Jauhar Trust were routed through contractors holding government contracts. A special PMLA court in Ghaziabad remanded Mr. Khan to judicial custody on November 1.

articles.title: Prince William says Gen Z is the torchbearer of the global movement for change
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II: Polity, Governance, Supreme Court Judgements, Bills & Govt Schemes
fullParagraphs: Young people from around the world are not waiting for someone else to find the solution, they are the torchbearers of the global movement for change, Britain’s Prince William said in Mumbai on Tuesday (November 17, 2026).
He was speaking at the 2026 Earthshot Prize Awards Ceremony, which was held in India for the first time.
Winners of the Earthshot Prize award were declared under five categories in a glittering ceremony. The awardees include the Himalayan Kingdom of Bhutan and Mahindra Last Mile Mobility.
“They [Gen Z] are bringing fresh ideas and showing what is possible when optimism is matched with action. Their ideas, their energy, and their determination are helping to shape the future,” he said.
During his address, Prince William reflected on the achievements of this year’s finalists and the growing global movement behind environmental innovation.
The ceremony was attended by environmental innovators, philanthropists, business leaders, government representatives and global figures from sport, entertainment and culture.
Mahindra Last Mile Mobility won the Earthshot Prize in the ‘Clean Our Air’ category. Accepting the award, the company’s CEO, Suman Mishra, said it showed how urgent optimism worked.
The company has won 1 million pounds for its efforts, due to which 33 per cent of India’s three-wheelers are now electric.
Prince Williams and Princess Catherine meet the winners of Earthshot Prize post the award ceremony in Mumbai on November 17, 2026. | Photo Credit: Emmanual Yogini
In the ‘Revive Our Oceans’ category, Niue Ocean Wide Trust was chosen for protecting the oceans, especially the vast Pacific region.
Coral Pasisi, vice chair and co-architect of Ocean Conservation Commitments, expressed gratitude for indigenous, people-led sustainability efforts being honoured.
“It is collective responsibility in action. We want to protect the oceans that protect us all,” she said while accepting the award.

articles.title: Cyclone Akvan: RMC forecasts moderate rainfall for Chennai on Wednesday
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II: Polity, Governance, Supreme Court Judgements, Bills & Govt Schemes
fullParagraphs: Even as Cyclone Akvan gathers strength over the Bay of Bengal, the Regional Meteorological Centre (RMC) here has forecast moderate rainfall at isolated places in Chennai, Tiruvallur and Chengalpattu districts on Wednesday.
Light rain is also likely at isolated places over south Tamil Nadu, the rest of north coastal Tamil Nadu, Puducherry and Karaikal. Dry weather is likely to prevail over the rest of the State.

For Thursday, the RMC has forecast heavy rain at isolated places in Chennai and Tiruvallur districts. Moderate rain is likely at isolated places in Chengalpattu, Kanchipuram, Villupuram and Cuddalore districts, as well as in Puducherry. Light rain is likely at isolated places over the Western Ghats districts. Dry weather is likely to prevail over the rest of the State and Karaikal.

Meanwhile, Cyclone Akvan moved northwestwards and lay centred at 8.30 a.m. on Tuesday about 610 km east of Chennai. It is very likely to move slowly north-northwestwards and intensify further into a severe cyclonic storm over the westcentral Bay of Bengal by the evening of November 17, 2026.

Thereafter, it is likely to move northwestwards and intensify into a very severe cyclonic storm by Thursday morning. The system is likely to cross the Andhra Pradesh and Yanam coasts between Nellore and Tuni around Thursday noon, with a maximum sustained wind speed of 120–130 kmph, gusting to 145 kmph.

articles.title: A poverty line that falls short
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Banking/SSC: RBI Monetary Policy, GDP, Inflation, Budget & Banking
fullParagraphs: There is no serious doubt that poverty in India has fallen sharply over the past decade. However, researchers and policymakers cannot agree on how many are still poor. Depending on the estimate, the share ranges from about 5% to more than 26%. Take the recent World Bank report. At its international line of $3 a day (2021 PPP), 2.6% of Indians were poor in 2022-23. Raise the line to $4.20, the bank’s benchmark for lower middle-income countries, and the figure jumps to around 16.1%. Same country, same year. Only the yardstick changed. A low level of extreme poverty does not necessarily mean poverty is not still a major issue. Where you draw the line decides how much economic insecurity you see.

India’s own figures tell a similar convoluted story. For example, SBI Research (2025) takes the Tendulkar line of 2009, adjusts it for inflation, and gets poverty of 7.2% in rural India and 4.6% in urban India for 2022-23. Rangarajan and Dev (2014), using an inflation-adjusted version of the Rangarajan Committee line, arrive at 10.8%. Further, Sethu, Surya and Ruthu (2024), who rebuild the Rangarajan method from the latest consumption survey, report 26.4%. Most of that gap boils down to the lines themselves: SBI’s Tendulkar-based lines use, after adjusting for inflation, about ₹1,632 a month per person in rural areas and ₹1,944 in urban areas. In contrast, Sethu et al. use much higher thresholds of ₹2,515 and ₹3,639. And the outcomes are obvious: Higher lines, higher poverty. Method matters too. One camp takes an old line and adjusts it for inflation. The other reconstructs the line from spending patterns in the new survey. Both have limitations, and they are answering different questions.

articles.title: Export duty on diesel hiked ₹2.5/litre, ATF ₹1.5/litre, petrol remains nil

fullParagraphs: The government late Monday (November 16, 2026) hiked the export duty on diesel and aviation turbine fuel (ATF) by ₹2.5 per litre and ₹1.5 per litre, whilst keeping the levy on export of petrol unchanged at nil.
Duty rates on petrol and diesel meant for domestic consumption remain unchanged.
The hike in diesel levy assumes added significance as India looks to further up their exports of the vehicular fuel to Europe amid a global supply crunch.
In the upcoming fortnight, diesel exports would draw a levy of ₹14 per litre compared to ₹11.5 per litre mandated for the previous fortnight.
ATF exports would draw a levy of ₹12.5 per litre against ₹11 per litre.

The government has been conducting a fortnightly review of export levies since March 27, in the backdrop of the conflict in West Asia. These are done based on the average international benchmark prices of crude oil, petrol, diesel and ATF observed since the previous review.
This is to ensure the domestic availability of retail fuels by disincentivising exports.

articles.title: Wholesale inflation rises to 12.3% in October 2026, second straight month of double-digit inflation
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Banking/SSC: RBI Monetary Policy, GDP, Inflation, Budget & Banking
fullParagraphs: Wholesale inflation in India surged to 12.3% in October 2026, the second consecutive month of double-digit inflation, official data released on Monday (November 16, 2026) showed. Fuel prices continue to be the main reason for the price rise, with the crude petroleum and natural gas sectors seeing inflation of more than 70%.

The new series of the Wholesale Price Index (WPI) by the Ministry of Commerce and Industry has data that goes back to only April 2024 and so a historical analysis for a longer duration is not possible. However, the data shows that inflation in October was the highest since at least then.
This data follows the release of Consumer Price Index data last week that showed that even retail inflation had climbed above the Reserve Bank of India’s upper comfort mark of 6% in October 2026.
According to Madan Sabnavis, chief economist at the Bank of Baroda, it is only a matter of time before wholesale inflation translates into a further increase in the prices consumers pay.

“It has been seen that manufactured goods in particular have witnessed an increase of 9.5%, with high inflation rates in textiles, tobacco products, chemicals, rubber products, metals and electrical equipment,” Mr. Sabnavis pointed out. “This will pressurise companies into increasing their product prices at some point of time.”
“This passthrough will get reflected in the core part of the CPI in the coming months depending on the actions of industry,” he added.

Further, as Payal V. Pandya, vice president at Bajaj Broking Prive argues, the high WPI inflation makes a rate hike by the RBI in December a near certainty, which would have a further dampening effect on the economy.

“The sharp rise in WPI inflation to 12.39% in October 2026 reinforces the inflationary concerns already reflected in elevated retail inflation readings,” Payal V. Pandya, vice president at Bajaj Broking Prive said. “As a result, a rate hike by the RBI in the upcoming Monetary Policy Committee meeting [in December] now looks almost certain.”

“Higher interest rates may impact lending activity, investments, and consumption, while sentiment across the financial sector could remain under pressure,” Ms. Pandya added. “With geopolitical tensions resurfacing in the Russia-Ukraine region, risks to inflation and economic growth have become even more pronounced.”

Within the WPI, food inflation climbed to 8.3% in October 2026, the highest in 22 months. The overall fuel and power category saw inflation jump to nearly 33% in the same month, compared to about 26% in September 2026. These high levels were, however, also a result of a low base, since this segment of the WPI was in contraction for large parts of 2025.
Similarly, the crude petroleum and natural gas segment saw inflation climb to 70.8% in October 2026 from 57.3% in September. This was compared to a 7.2% contraction in prices in October of last year.

articles.title: Iron ore capacity under-utilisation in major-producing states prompt concerns as India sets 2047 target
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Banking/SSC: RBI Monetary Policy, GDP, Inflation, Budget & Banking
fullParagraphs: With India’s iron ore demand projected to rise to 772 million tonnes (MT) by 2047, miners in Odisha, the country’s largest iron ore reserve holder, are yet to utilise nearly 40% of their existing capacities, raising concerns over resource wastage and potential revenue losses.
The issue has come under judicial scrutiny, with both the Supreme Court earlier this month and the Odisha High Court in January flagging the underutilisation of mining capacities.

The Odisha High Court, while agreeing with petitioners who highlighted the sluggish operationalisation of mines despite environmental clearances, observed that the delay had resulted in an average annual revenue loss of ₹4,000 crore to the State.
However, industry sources, speaking on condition of anonymity, attributed the delays primarily to prolonged forest clearance procedures, which often exceed the stipulated 18-month timeframe.

Data cited by petitioner Citizens’ Action Forum (Bhubaneswar) show that of the 246 million tonnes per annum (MTPA) of mining capacity granted environmental clearance in FY25, only around 159 MTPA had been operationalised.

Separately, data published by mining consultancy BigMint in June 2026 show that Odisha produced 158 MT of iron ore in FY26 against an environmentally cleared capacity of 278 MTPA, indicating capacity utilisation of nearly 60%.
The underutilised capacity is particularly significant as it largely involves hematite, which is among the highest-grade varieties of iron ore

The shortfall also raises questions over India’s continued dependence on imports. According to the Mines Ministry, the country imported 12.3 MT of iron ore in FY26, incurring an expenditure of ₹11,115 crore.

Odisha accounted for more than 50% of India’s domestic iron ore production during FY26. Chhattisgarh contributed around 17.1%, followed by Karnataka at 16.6%. Capacity utilisation in the two states – albeit with significantly lower volumes than Odisha – stood at 62% and 80%, respectively, according to calculations based on BigMint data.

In January, the Odisha High Court directed that mining rights be mandatorily transferred to state-owned National Mineral Development Corporation (NMDC) to ensure “optimum utilisation of the mines” and “eradicate any burden on the government exchequer”.

However, in its November 4 order, the Supreme Court concurred with the need for optimum utilisation of mineral resources but left the decision on transferring mining rights to the State government’s discretion, rather than making it mandatory.

articles.title: Nabeel Rajab, prominent Bahraini human rights activist, dies at 62
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Current Affairs: Bilateral Agreements, Foreign Visits & UN/G20/BRICS
fullParagraphs: Nabeel Rajab, a prominent democracy activist in Bahrain who helped lead the island nation's 2011 protests known across the wider region as the Arab Spring and who spent years in prison for challenging its monarchy, died on Tuesday (November 17, 2026). He was 62.

His family found him unresponsive at their home in Turkey on Tuesday (November 17, 2026) morning, activists said. The Bahrain Center for Human Rights, which Rajab once led as president, confirmed his death in a post on X.

"We extend our sincere condolences and heartfelt sympathy to his esteemed family. We pray that God may encompass him with his vast mercy and reward him abundantly for his efforts and contributions," the group wrote.

Ebrahim Sharif, an activist who was a close friend of the family, said Rajab's wife and daughter found him unresponsive early in the morning at their home in Turkey. He said he had spoken to Rajab's brother and that the family believed Rajab likely died of a heart attack.

Rajab left Bahrain early in the Iran war, as authorities cracked down on Shia-led protests throughout the Gulf island kingdom, home to the U.S. Navy's Fifth Fleet. Rajab accused the government of torturing an imprisoned activist and feared he would be arrested if he returned, he told The Associated Press at the time.

Rajab rose to international prominence in 2011, as the Arab Spring uprising swept the region and demonstrations erupted in Bahrain's capital, Manama. He was a pivotal figure in the protest movement, during which the country's majority Shiite population demanded the ruling Sunni monarchy offer them greater political freedoms. As president of the Bahrain Centre for Human Rights, he advocated for expanding the powers of Bahrain's parliament, ensuring freedom of expression and fighting anti-Shia discrimination.
Bahraini authorities, backed by Saudi troops, arrested scores of demonstrators and crushed the protests, while ultimately introducing limited political reforms.

He was imprisoned on multiple occasions in the years following the unrest. His longest stretch behind bars began in June 2016. He was eventually released in June of 2020 during the coronavirus pandemic, though he was ordered to spend the remaining time in home detention.

At the time, he had been serving a five-year sentence over tweets criticising the Saudi-led war in Yemen and alleging prison abuse. He had also been sentenced to two years over comments deemed critical of Bahrain.

Rajab had a history of heart issues. During one of his earlier detentions, he received treatment for an irregular heartbeat. He separately received a pardon from King Hamad bin Isa Al Khalifa in 2015, after concerns emerged about Rajab's health.

articles.title: Ukraine strikes major Russian bridge with drones and missiles as aerial attacks escalate
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Current Affairs: Bilateral Agreements, Foreign Visits & UN/G20/BRICS
fullParagraphs: U krainian drones and missiles struck a vital bridge linking Russia to the occupied Crimean Peninsula, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on Tuesday (November 17, 2026), calling it an "unprecedented" operation as Russia reported that its forces downed a record number of Ukrainian drones for the second straight day.

Mr. Zelenskyy portrayed the operation on the Kerch Bridge as a masterstroke, as Ukrainian forces gradually wore down Russian air defenses for weeks before bombarding the prized target with a barrage of missiles and drones overnight.

Mr. Zelenskyy didn't detail the damage, but the Ukrainian General Staff said an arch and a span of the bridge's road section collapsed, severing the road link, while the railway line was still standing but its arch was damaged.

The Kerch Bridge is a crucial link in moving military and civilian supplies from Russia to Crimea and to support troops on the front line. The construction of the bridge, a potent symbol of Russia's illegal annexation of the peninsula in 2014, was inflammatory for Ukrainians.
"The symbol of the occupation has cracked," the Ukrainian General Staff said in a statement.
Moscow's forces, meanwhile, fired ballistic missiles and drones at Kyiv, hitting two of the Ukrainian capital's main bridges and killing at least two people.

A recent escalation in aerial attacks came as Russia and Ukraine await a date for the next round of U.S.-mediated talks aimed at ending the war that began with Moscow's full-scale invasion of its neighbour on February 24, 2022.

U.S. President Donald Trump says he plans to talk about the war in Ukraine during his highly anticipated meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin in China this week.
The Kerch Bridge attack was the culmination of weeks of preparatory strikes over seven stages of the operation, Mr. Zelenskyy said on social media.
Ukrainian forces knocked out defense systems, radars, electronic warfare equipment and other designated targets before launching Monday night's final attack, he said.

Domestically developed long-range drones struck the bridge's road section during the night while Ukraine's Neptune missiles and other drones aimed at the rail section, he said. Flamingo precision-guided missiles delivered the final blow, he said.
Russia's Investigative Committee said the bridge was attacked by drones and sustained damage. It didn't elaborate.

articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Current Affairs: Bilateral Agreements, Foreign Visits & UN/G20/BRICS
fullParagraphs: Iran launched a fresh drone attack against Bahrain on Tuesday (November 17, 2026) and dismissed a report alleging a dirty-bomb plot against the United States, which President Donald Trump said he took "very seriously".

Mediator Qatar urged "all parties" to show restraint following an uptick in hostilities, with Bahrain targeted three times in five days after a lull in Iranian attacks on Gulf countries since September.

Mr. Trump was speaking after CNN cited seven anonymous U.S. officials as saying Iran was plotting to target senior administration figures with a "dirty" bomb, laced with chemical or radioactive materials.
"If there is [such a threat], they will pay a price the likes of which no other country has ever paid before," Trump said after arriving for a summit in the Philippines.
"I hope it's not, but we take it very seriously because they happen to be crazy."
Iran's Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baqaei dismissed the report as "fabricated".

"Those who initiated the aggression against Iran are now seeking to lay the media groundwork for their sinister designs by manufacturing and disseminating baseless allegations" including "the fabricated media narrative surrounding an alleged 'dirty bomb' propagated by CNN", he posted on X.
Mr. Baqaei also criticised a New York Times report questioning whether Iranian dams and water projects had military uses.
Earlier on Tuesday (November 17, 2026), explosions boomed across Bahrain's capital as a mobile-phone alert warned residents to seek safety.

Bahrain's armed forces said they "confronted, intercepted and destroyed a number of treacherous Iranian aerial attacks today... before they could achieve their objectives", while Iran's Revolutionary Guards said they targeted a U.S.-operated radar system.

"Combat drones belonging to the Revolutionary Guards carried out a precision operation this morning, targeting a radar system operated by US forces at the Sheikh Isa Air Base in Bahrain," the Guards' Sepah news website said.

The attack was in response to the "repeated violations of Iranian airspace by US military drones", it added. The Guards also said they had intercepted and captured a US drone south of Qeshm island in the Strait of Hormuz.

articles.title: Bangladesh connects first nuclear power plant to national grid
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Current Affairs: Bilateral Agreements, Foreign Visits & UN/G20/BRICS
fullParagraphs: Bangladesh's first nuclear power plant at Rooppur in the country's northwest Pabna district began supplying electricity to the national grid on a trial basis on Tuesday (November 17, 2026), according to officials.
The 2,400 MW Russian-assisted facility is expected to meet more than 10% of Bangladesh's electricity demand once fully operational, helping the country diversify its energy sources.
“We have become the 33rd country in the world to produce and generate nuclear power,” Science and Technology Minister Fakir Mahbub Anam told reporters at the plant site.
The development comes as the South Asian nation of 170 million people grapples with a fuel crisis triggered by the conflict in West Asia.
The plant comprises two units, each with a generation capacity of 1,200 MW, officials said, adding that the first unit has begun supplying 350 MW of electricity to the national grid.

According to the Science and Technology Ministry, the initial connection would last between eight and 10 hours, during which engineers would conduct tests on the plant's turbine, generator and grid stability.
The unit would subsequently be disconnected for further technical tests and could be reconnected after about 28 hours for another four to six hours to complete additional operational checks.
Under an agreement with the Russian contractor, the first unit will undergo a 10-month trial operation before beginning commercial electricity generation at full capacity, the ministry said.
Construction on the facility began in 2017 during the administration of ousted prime minister Sheikh Hasina, following a 2015 agreement with Moscow.

articles.title: India cannot dictate terms on Hasina’s return to Bangladesh: PM’s adviser
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Current Affairs: Bilateral Agreements, Foreign Visits & UN/G20/BRICS
fullParagraphs: Bangladesh Prime Minister Tarique Rahman’s Information Adviser Zahed Ur Rahman on Tuesday (November 17, 2026) said that India or any other country could not dictate terms over deposed Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina’s return home.

"Neither India nor any other country can dictate terms on this,” Mr. Zahed said during a media briefing when asked for comments on a media report saying New Delhi had hinted at two conditions for handing over Hasina.
Hasina has been staying in India since fleeing the country in August 2024 following a student-led uprising that toppled her government.
Talking to reporters at the Bangladesh Secretariat, Mr. Zahed said, “Bangladesh is now an independent, sovereign state standing on firm legal ground and it will reject any unjust terms.”
The premier’s Adviser, however, said he did not believe India would attach conditions to returning Hasina.
On Friday (November 13, 2026), Ministry of External Affairs spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal said Hasina's extradition was a legal matter and would be dealt with accordingly.
He further said: “India desires a positive, constructive and forward-looking relationship with Bangladesh."
Bangladesh's International Crimes Tribunal convicted Hasina in November 2025 of crimes against humanity for her role in the crackdown on protesters during the July-August 2024 uprising.
Tried in absentia, she was sentenced to death on one charge and life imprisonment on another. Hasina has rejected the charges and the proceedings.

In a report last week, BBC Bangla said unnamed Indian officials indicated that New Delhi set two main conditions to facilitate Hasina’s return amid Dhaka’s repeated insistence on her extradition under a bilateral treaty despite her repeated stated plan to return home voluntarily to face the legal procedure.
The report said that “under the conditions, India wanted Bangladesh Army to directly receive Hasina either via a military flight to Delhi or at a land border crossing”.
It said New Delhi simultaneously demanded judicial safeguards on her return, seeking assurances that she would receive the right to appeal her death penalty and undergo a fresh trial.

articles.title: ‘Record horticultural production’ shows increase of 4.36% from 2024-25: Agriculture Ministry
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Prelims: ISRO/NASA Missions, Defense Updates, Tech & Climate Reports
fullParagraphs: India’s total horticultural production is expected to reach 3,869.15 lakh tonnes in 2025-26, an increase of 161.77 lakh tonnes (4.36%) over the production recorded in 2024-25, according to the third advanced estimates of area and production of horticultural crops released by Union Agriculture Minister Shivraj Singh Chouhan in New Delhi on Tuesday (November 17, 2026). In the previous crop season, horticulture production stood at 3,707.38 lakh tonnes.

Mr. Chouhan expressed satisfaction over the projected growth and said the significant increase in horticultural production reflected the hard work of India’s farmers and the impact of the Union government’s farmer-friendly policies. “This record production would not only strengthen the country’s nutritional security but also directly contribute to higher incomes for horticulture farmers,” the Minister said, congratulating farmers across the country for their efforts.

Farmers were increasingly moving beyond traditional crops towards the cultivation of fruits, vegetables, flowers, spices, and plantation crops, including cashew, coconut and cocoa, as well as aromatic and medicinal plants, he said.

“This growing interest in commercial and high-value crops is opening up new avenues of income for farmers while creating fresh opportunities for self-reliance and growth in the agricultural sector,” Mr. Chouhan said, adding that one of the most significant aspects of the latest estimates was increase in production despite a reduction in the area under horticultural cultivation.

“The total area under horticultural crops in 2025-26 is estimated at approximately 297.21 lakh hectares, compared with 301.36 lakh hectares in 2024-25. Despite the decline in cultivated area, production is projected to increase across fruits, vegetables, flowers, plantation crops, and aromatic and medicinal plants,” Mr. Chouhan said.

Fruit production is estimated to rise from 1,176.49 lakh tonnes in 2024-25 to 1,230.66 lakh tonnes in 2025-26, an increase of 54.18 lakh tonnes or 4.60%. “The improved output is primarily attributed to better production of banana, mango, papaya, apple, pomegranate and jackfruit,” the Union Agriculture Ministry said in a release.

The area under vegetables is estimated to increase from 117.91 lakh hectares to 119.31 lakh hectares. “Vegetable production is projected to rise by 4.35%, from 2,177.97 lakh tonnes in 2024-25 to 2,272.68 lakh tonnes in 2025-26. The increase is primarily driven by higher production of potato, tomato, brinjal, bottle gourd, cucumber, cabbage, beans and peas,” the release added. Potato and tomato production are both expected to register strong growth. Potato production is estimated at 655.70 lakh tonnes, up 11.95% from 585.71 lakh tonnes in the previous year. Tomato production is projected to increase from 205.99 lakh tonnes to 214.11 lakh tonnes. Onion production is estimated at 288.96 lakh tonnes.

Flower production is projected to rise by approximately 14.45%, from 42.65 lakh tonnes in 2024-25 to 48.82 lakh tonnes in 2025-26. “The area under flower cultivation has also increased to 4.10 lakh hectares,” it added. In the production of plantation crops, including arecanut, coconut, cashew, betel leaves and cocoa. “Their combined production is estimated to increase by 7.56% to 182.64 lakh tonnes. Production of aromatic and medicinal plants is also expected to rise from 9.01 lakh tonnes to 9.28 lakh tonnes,” the Ministry of Agriculture added.

The production of turmeric, garlic, curry leaves and cardamom is also expected to grow. “The total area under spices in 2025-26 is estimated at 47.56 lakh hectares, with production projected at 123.54 lakh tonnes,” the Ministry said.

articles.title: Hospital in Chennai performs complex aortic surgery on 10-year-old boy with rare vascular disease
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Prelims: ISRO/NASA Missions, Defense Updates, Tech & Climate Reports
fullParagraphs: A 10-year-old with a rare inflammatory blood vessel disease underwent surgery at SIMS Hospital, Chennai, to repair a large aneurysm of the aortic arch, the hospital said on Tuesday (November 17, 2026).

The patient was diagnosed with aortoarteritis, also known as Takayasu arteritis, a condition that causes inflammation and narrowing or enlargement of blood vessels. The aneurysm had enlarged significantly, causing breathing difficulty, palpitations, and difficulty lying down. The risk of rupture made urgent surgery necessary. The patient weighed about 18 kg, adding to the technical challenges of the operation. As the aneurysm was located close to the breastbone, opening the chest through the usual approach carried a risk of injuring the enlarged aorta. The surgical team first connected the patient to a heart-lung machine through blood vessels in the groin.

The patient’s body was cooled to 16°C using a technique known as deep hypothermic circulatory arrest. Blood circulation was then temporarily stopped for about 40 minutes, enabling surgeons to remove the affected section of the aorta and replace it with a Dacron graft. Lowering the body temperature reduces metabolic activity and the organs’ oxygen requirements, helping protect them during the period when blood flow is interrupted.

The patient was subsequently rewarmed, restoring his blood circulation. Post-operative assessments showed no damage to the brain, kidneys, intestines, or spinal cord, the hospital said. The patient has resumed normal activities without breathing difficulty but will require continued medication and monitoring to control the underlying inflammation and prevent further aneurysms.

The surgery was performed by a team led by Bashi V. Velayudhan, director and senior consultant, cardiothoracic surgery, along with Mohammed Idhrees, senior consultant, cardiothoracic surgery, and a team of anaesthesiologists and other specialists.
